title: Confession rites
hook: from the Orthodox confession before an icon to the general confession in a prayer book

segments.voice: Yesterday, unction: a little case of oil, a hospital corridor, and the elders coming when called. Your line was oil and prayer.

In a small Orthodox church, a woman stands at a lectern near the front, facing an icon of Christ, with a Gospel book and a cross resting there. The priest stands beside her, not across from her. She speaks quietly. When she's finished, she bows her head, and he lays the end of his stole over it and prays. Across town, in a church with a prayer book in every pew, a whole congregation kneels, and every voice says the same words at once: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done."

Christians confess in different rooms, leaning on the same two lines. The first comes one verse after yesterday's oil: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." In James, confession is spoken out loud to another person. The second is from the first letter of John: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Now, three rooms. First, the Orthodox. The person confessing stands before an icon of Christ, the priest beside them, and in some Orthodox prayers before confession the priest describes himself as only a witness: it's Christ who hears and forgives. Second, the Catholic sacrament of penance, often called reconciliation. A person tells their sins to a priest in private, behind a screen or face to face, and hears the words of absolution. The priest is bound by the seal of confession: he may never repeat what he heard. Third, the general confession, said together from the old English prayer book: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done." Some Protestant services include a prayer of confession like it, followed by words of forgiveness. Notice the order: left undone comes first, the good nobody got around to, the visit, the apology, the help. In every room the shape is the same. Say it out loud. Hear that it's forgiven.

Don't make a list; look for just one thing, something you did, or, following the prayer book, something you left undone: the call you didn't make, the thank-you never said. Name it plainly to yourself, without excuses and without piling on. If you pray, bring it to God and rest on John's promise, faithful and just to forgive; if you don't, let it be named, and notice what changes when it is.
Confession rites. The church's ways of saying sin out loud and hearing it forgiven: before an icon, to a priest, or all together.
Your line: we have left undone. The good undone gets named first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians confess before an icon of Christ with a priest beside them; Catholics confess privately to a priest in the sacrament of penance and receive absolution; Anglican, Lutheran and some other Protestant services include a general confession said together, followed by a declaration of forgiveness.

options: say nothing and hope it fades.

chat.says: Is confession always one person whispering in a dark booth?
options: No; some confess before an icon, some privately to a priest, some all together from a prayer book.
Yes; every church requires a private booth, and saying it together doesn't count at all.
No; it's only ever silent, since saying sins out loud to anyone is never part of it.
chat.meaning: Orthodox Christians confess before an icon, Catholics privately to a priest, and prayer-book churches together. Each says sin out loud and hears it forgiven.

stole.meaning: a long strip of cloth a priest wears

absolution.meaning: a priest's words of forgiveness after confession

seal of confession.meaning: the rule that a priest never repeats what he heard

penance.meaning: the Catholic sacrament of confession, often called reconciliation

notes: Hook: Orthodox scene (icon, Gospel book and cross on a stand, priest beside the penitent, epitrachelion laid over the head with the prayer of absolution) given as one scene; practice varies by jurisdiction. Confirm.
'In some Orthodox prayers before confession, the priest describes himself as only a witness' paraphrases the exhortation used in Slavonic-tradition churches; confirm.
BCP 1662 General Confession (Morning Prayer) quoted; confirm exact capitalization and punctuation.
'Many Protestant services include a prayer of confession' — confirm or soften to 'some'.
Original: ἐξομολογεῖσθε (present imperative, James 5:16); confirm accent and transliteration.

Audit pass: 'left undone comes first' overstated the text: the 1662 General Confession already confesses wrongs done ('followed too much the devices and desires of our own hearts', 'offended against thy holy laws') before this pair. Teach, screen head, myth and trapdoor now say 'within the pair'. Doubled 'small' in the hook cut.
Editor pass: garbled 'stands at a stand' fixed; James 5:16 is an instruction, so 'two promises' became 'two lines'; 'many Protestant services' softened to 'some'.
